result.summary: Ulysses tells how Aeolus gave him the winds in a sack, which his men opened, and how the Laestrygonians destroyed all his ships but his own. He then reaches Circe's island, where she turns his scouts into pigs. With Mercury's herb Moly he overcomes her, frees his men, stays a year, and is told to consult Teiresias in the house of Hades.

scenes.title: Aeolus and the bag of winds
scenes.summary: Aeolus entertains Ulysses and gives him the winds in an ox-hide sack. Within sight of Ithaca the men open it, and a storm drives them back.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses is about to reach home, but his men's greed and his own sleep wreck the voyage.

scenes.title: Aeolus refuses help
scenes.summary: Ulysses begs Aeolus for help again, but Aeolus drives him away as hated by the gods.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses loses his last chance of a quick return home.

scenes.title: Laestrygonians destroy the fleet
scenes.summary: The fleet enters the Laestrygonian harbour. Antiphates and his people kill the crews and sink the ships, and only Ulysses' ship escapes.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses and his men risk being killed and eaten by giants.

scenes.title: Arrival at Aeaea; the stag
scenes.summary: Ulysses reaches Circe's island, kills a stag to feed his men, and divides them into two companies. Eurylochus' group goes to explore.
scenes.stakes: The crew are exhausted and lost, and fear another deadly encounter.

scenes.title: Circe turns men to pigs
scenes.summary: Circe feeds Eurylochus' company drugged food and turns them into pigs. Eurylochus escapes and reports, and Ulysses sets out alone.
scenes.stakes: Twenty-two men are enchanted, and Ulysses risks the same fate.

scenes.title: Mercury, Moly and Circe's defeat
scenes.summary: Mercury gives Ulysses the herb Moly and instructions. Ulysses resists Circe's drug, threatens her with his sword, and makes her swear an oath.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses risks being turned into a pig or unmanned.

scenes.title: Men restored; Eurylochus rebuked
scenes.summary: Circe's maids bathe and feed Ulysses, and he demands his men's release. Circe restores them, and the rest of the crew come to the house despite Eurylochus' protest.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses' men must be freed and the crew kept united.

scenes.title: Journey to Hades ordered
scenes.summary: After a year the men urge departure. Circe tells Ulysses to consult Teiresias in Hades and explains the rites. Elpenor falls to his death, and the crew grieve.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses must visit the dead to learn the way home.

notable_quotes.reason: Describes the magical herb Moly, root of a famous literary allusion.
Memorable line on the unseen movements of the gods.

analysis.text: Ulysses' fortunes turn on trust and discipline: the crew's greed ruins the winds' gift, and Circe's episode tests his caution against temptation.
The episode reflects Greek ideas of hospitality and its limits, and the wide Mediterranean geography imagined by early sailors.

legacy.text: Circe's transformation of men into animals became a lasting literary motif, treated by Ovid and later writers.
The herb Moly became a standard literary symbol of protection against enchantment, used by Milton in Comus.

fun_facts.text: Ancient tradition located Circe's island at Monte Circeo on the Italian coast, though it is actually a headland.

language_notes.text: Aeolian island: the home of Aeolus, keeper of the winds. Aeolus here is a mortal-seeming king whom Jove has appointed ruler of the winds.
The "83" is a footnote marker from the edition, not part of the story. "Girds" means encircles.
"Till it groans again, yard and all" means the courtyard and house seem to groan under the heavy smell of cooking meat.
"Further me on my way" means help me continue my journey.
"Flayed" means skinned. Aeolus skinned an ox to make the hide bag.
"Dead beat" is a colloquial phrase meaning exhausted.
"Bless my heart" is a mild, colloquial exclamation of surprise, a modern-sounding touch in this translation.
Sitting as suppliants on the threshold was a formal plea for protection and help; hosts were bound by custom to respect it.
Ulysses refers to his men opening Aeolus' bag of winds while he slept, which blew the fleet back from sight of Ithaca.
"Him whom heaven hates will I in no wise help" is inverted, archaic word order meaning 'I will in no way help one whom the gods hate.'
The odd detail of shepherds greeting each other describes a place where day and night nearly meet, as in the far north with short nights.
"To reconnoitre" means to scout an area to gather information.
A "hue-and-cry" is a loud public outcry calling people to chase a wrongdoer.
Aeetes is the magician king of Colchis, known from the Argonauts' story of the Golden Fleece. Circe is his sister, and their father is the sun god Helios.
"Reconnoitre" means to scout an area to gather information before acting.
A fathom is about six feet, so the rope is roughly that length.
Uncovering their heads was a gesture of respect and wonder, as men pulled their cloaks from their faces to look at the stag.
"Child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn" is a fixed Homeric formula for daybreak.
Refers to earlier disasters in this book: the Laestrygonians under Antiphates destroyed most of the fleet, and Polyphemus the Cyclops ate several men.
"Drugged into subjection" means she used potions to make the animals tame and obedient; they were evidently once men or ordinary beasts changed by her.
"Staid" is an old spelling of "stayed."
Pramnian wine was a strong, well-known wine of the ancient Greek world; here it is the base for Circe's drugged drink.
A "mess" is an old term for a prepared dish of food, here a porridge-like mixture.
"Beech masts" are beechnuts, the fallen fruit of the beech tree, used as pig feed.
"Whither" is archaic for "to where"; Mercury asks where Ulysses thinks he is going.
"Virtue" here means power or potency, not moral goodness. A "talisman" is an object that protects against harm.
"Point blank refuse" means refuse flatly. "Unman" means strip him of strength and manhood, leaving him helpless.
Moly is a magical plant named by the gods. Its identity is unknown; the text only says mortals cannot uproot it.
A "mess" is a prepared dish or mixture; here it is a drugged potion of meal and other ingredients.
Circe recalls a prophecy from Mercury that Ulysses would come on his way home from Troy, where he fought in the Trojan War.
Circe's maids are nymphs, minor female nature spirits tied to groves, springs and rivers in Greek belief.
The superscript "87" is a footnote marker from the edition, not part of Ulysses' speech.
A ewer is a large jug for pouring water; guests washed their hands before eating.
"Halloa-ballooing" is the translator's playful coinage for loud, noisy shouting.
"Keep guard over her house" means they would be kept as beast-guardians, like the wolves and lions Ulysses' men met earlier at Circe's door.
Refers to the earlier episode in the Cyclops Polyphemus' cave, where several of Ulysses' men were eaten.
"In two minds" means undecided; "near relation" notes that Eurylochus is a kinsman of Ulysses.
"If so be" is archaic for "if it is indeed the case that"; the men doubt Ulysses will survive to see home.
"Besought her by her knees" refers to the suppliant's gesture of clasping the knees of the one petitioned.
Proserpine is the Roman name for the queen of the dead (the Greek Persephone), wife of Hades.
Oceanus is the great river thought to encircle the world, at whose edge lies the land of the dead.
A cubit is an ancient measure of about the length of a forearm, roughly 18 inches.
Erebus is the dark region of the underworld where the dead dwell.
Gossamer means a very fine, light, filmy cloth; a girdle is a belt or sash.
"Did not mend matters" means their weeping changed nothing about the situation.

context_notes.text: The marriage of brothers and sisters is unusual and marks Aeolus's household as strange and set apart from ordinary human society.
Argive and Achaeans both refer to the Greeks who fought at Troy. Aeolus wants news of the war.
Jove (the Greek Zeus) is king of the gods. Here he has given Aeolus power to calm or raise each wind.
Aeolus is the keeper of the winds, who earlier hosted Ulysses and gave him a bag containing the adverse winds.
The Laestrygonians are a race of giant cannibals; Lamus is their legendary founder and Telepylus their city.
Ulysses' ship alone was moored outside the harbour, which let him cut the cable and flee.
Circe is a goddess and sorceress who will turn men into animals. Oceanus, the great river encircling the world, is her grandfather.
Eurylochus is Ulysses' second-in-command and brother-in-law. He later becomes the one who warns Ulysses of Circe's danger.
Circe is a goddess and enchantress living on the island of Aeaea. Ulysses' men are exploring it after landing.
Polites is one of Ulysses' companions, here singled out as especially trusted.
Ulysses arms himself and sets out alone to rescue his men. On the way he will meet Mercury, who gives him a protective herb.
Mercury (the Greek Hermes) is the gods' messenger and a guide of travellers, known for his golden wand and for helping heroes.
Olympus is the mountain home of the gods.
Bathing, fresh clothes and a seat of honour were standard hospitality for a guest in Homeric society.
Laertes was Ulysses' father; "son of Laertes" is a formal address (patronymic).
Eurylochus is Ulysses' second-in-command; he had escaped Circe's trap and brought the news of the men's transformation.
Teiresias was a blind prophet of Thebes, famed for his foresight; only he keeps his wits among the dead.
Offerings of blood and food were thought to give the shadowy dead strength to speak.
Flat roofs were used for sleeping in warm weather, which explains why Elpenor was up there.

literary_notes.text: The floating island with its iron-bound wall gives a sense of a magical, unreal place.
The remark that it all came to nothing because of the crew's folly warns the listener of disaster before it is told.
Ulysses stays awake to hurry home, yet his single lapse into sleep, just before arrival, causes the failure.
The crew's grumbling, in direct speech, shows their envy and suspicion, and makes their later mistake believable.
The wind is described as flying and howling forth, as though a living creature were released from captivity.
Aeolus, who once welcomed Ulysses, now treats him as accursed; the sudden reversal shows how a hero's fortune can turn.
Speared "like fishes" turns the men into catch, making the giants' slaughter both vivid and degrading.
The flat, brief line states the loss of eleven ships and their crews without comment, which heightens the horror.
A god conveniently sends the stag, showing the epic idea that the gods guide and aid heroes in need.
The formulaic dawn description marks the passing of time in the traditional style of oral epic.
The tears as Eurylochus' party leaves hint that the exploration will end badly.
The fawning beasts are compared to hounds greeting a master returning from dinner, making the strange scene seem tame while still unsettling.
Circe's beautiful singing and fine woven web create a pleasing, domestic image that hides her danger.
Eurylochus' suspicion, set against the others' trusting innocence, signals that danger waits inside the house.
The men's bodies become pigs but their minds stay human, which makes the transformation more cruel and pitiable.
Eurylochus' fearful pleading shows him as cautious and self-preserving, contrasting with Ulysses' resolve.
Comparing the transformed men to wild boars in lairs stresses how Circe has degraded them to animals.
The contrast of black root and milk-white flower, plus divine-only knowledge, marks Moly as a gift of the gods, beyond human power.
Circe unknowingly confirms Mercury's plan: her recognition of Ulysses shows the god foresaw everything, while she thinks she has been undone by chance.
Circe's second drug undoes the first and leaves the men better than before, turning her cruelty into an unexpected gift.
The joyful men are compared to calves frisking around their mothers, an image of homely, farmyard happiness.
Calling the men "affectionate creatures" shows Ulysses' fond, slightly amused view of his crew, echoing the animal imagery.
Ulysses' near-murderous anger at Eurylochus shows his fierce command, tempered by the crew's pleading.
The line echoes sentence 140's formula, marking the year's passing and the repeated pattern of Ulysses yielding to others' wishes.
Ulysses' wish to die rather than see the sun again conveys the depth of his despair at the order.
Elpenor is introduced as foolish and unremarkable, preparing his careless, undignified death.
Ulysses as narrator closes with a reflective aside on divine power, suggesting gods move unseen among mortals.
